title: How Much Money Do MLM Participants Actually Make?

sentences.text: Somewhere in your messages there is probably a pitch like this.
A friend you have not heard from in years has started a business, and she would love to have you on her team: you earn from what you sell, and from everyone you bring in after you.
The recruiters have a word for that second part: one trainer, Frazer Brookes, promises to show you how to "finally create the leverage that you need inside of your network marketing business".

sentences.text: So where does the money go, and why does leverage that sounds so good on paper show up in almost nobody's bank account?
This video is about one question: how much money do people in multi-level marketing actually make?

onScreenText: How much money do MLM participants actually make?

sentences.text: To answer it we have the companies' own numbers first: 70 income disclosure statements, read closely by Federal Trade Commission staff.
Then a nationally representative survey of 601 participants by AARP.
And an analysis of 30 companies by Jon Taylor, an independent analyst who argues against the industry.

sentences.text: First, the promise, in the recruiters' own words: one coach, Darin Kidd, tells his audience that once the team grows, "it starts to compound", like a snowball; Frazer Brookes says the person you bring in "might recruit 10 people themselves and have an organization of a thousand people".
Another trainer, Eric Worre, puts the whole idea in one line: it would be "better to have a smaller percentage of 100 people than 100 of yourself".

sentences.text: Two confident stories, so let us see which one the numbers tell.
Start with the companies, because some of them publish an income disclosure statement, and FTC staff collected 70 of them, from household names to small firms.

excerpt.text: The FTC staff report documents an analysis of 70 publicly available income disclosure statements from a wide range of MLMs — big and well-known to smaller companies. The report found that these income disclosure statements showed most participants made $1,000 or less per year — that’s less than $84 dollars per month. And that may not account for expenses. In at least 17 MLMs, most participants didn’t make any money at all.

sentences.text: First, who gets counted: of the 70 statements, 29 leave out participants who earned no commission, and another 24 leave out anyone the company has labelled inactive.
What happens to an average when you remove the zeros before you take it?

sentences.text: Disclosures count what companies paid, not whether anyone came out ahead; for that you have to ask the people.
AARP did, in a study published in 2018, using a probability-based national panel, the kind of sample that lets you generalise to the whole country.
Among the 601 people it reached, 47 percent said they lost money, 27 percent said they broke even, and the rest, a quarter, said they made a profit, counting their entire time in the business.

sentences.text: So most people lose or break even, and the few who profit mostly profit a little. The pitch said recruiting would compound, so why doesn't it?

The FTC describes how the pay plans typically work: commissions for hitting benchmarks such as buying a set amount of product, getting others to buy it, or recruiting people who then buy it; selling to an outside customer at a markup is mentioned as a source of income "in some cases".

sentences.text: Taylor went further: he read the compensation plans of the 30 companies with published earnings data, and of more than 350 in all, and concluded that each of them pays primarily for recruiting a large downline rather than for retailing product, with most of the payout going to the highest levels.
That is one analyst's reading of the plans; the FTC's report describes the same structure but does not measure how much income actually comes from downlines versus retail customers.

excerpt.text:
Based on my analysis of their compensation plans, using the four causal and defining
characteristics ("red flags")10 as a checklist, ALL (100%) of the 30 MLMs included in this
analysis are recruitment driven and top-weighted. This means that rewards are paid
primarily for the aggressive recruitment of a large downline, not for retailing products; and
most of the money paid by the company goes to participants at the highest levels. I have
analyzed the compensation plans of over 350 MLMs and found that ALL (100%) are
recruitment-driven and top-weighted, so it seems justifiable to assume that the same results
could be expected for other MLMs.11

sentences.text: His own estimate is blunter: across those companies, after subtracting required purchases and modest expenses, he puts the share losing money at 99.6 percent, about one in 238 profiting.

That number depends on his assumptions about what participants had to spend, how many dropped out and how many were ever counted, which he states; it is an estimate built on the companies' tables, not a measurement of anyone's bank account.
